mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Samantabhadra ‌place universal ​good, ​practice at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living mythological ​world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

Samantabhadra ​appears ‌in buddhist ​tradition ‌as universal ​good, ​practice. The ​name's ​meaning, "'Universal ​Beneficence' ‌— the ​Bodhisattva ‌of practice, ​rider ‌of the ​white ‌elephant", shapes ​the ‌narratives told ​about ​this figure.

### ‌Worship ‌and ‌Memory (Cult)

​Devotees ​and later ‌tradition-keepers ​preserved Samantabhadra ​in ‌ritual, text, ​and ​iconography, ensuring ‌the ​name survived ‌into ​the modern ​scholarly ​record.

The ​myths ‌of Samantabhadra ‌survive ​in fragments, ‌summaries, ​and ​later retellings. ‌Each ‌version reflects ‌the ‌interests of ​its ‌tellers — ​poets, ​priests, philosophers, ​and ‌scholars. The ​PuniCodex ​entry does ​not ‌privilege a ​single ​version; it ​gathers ‌the attestations ​so ‌that readers ​can ‌compare ​them. The ‌restoration ‌Samantabhadra gives ​the ​figure a ​stable ​name around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

overview.body:
**Samantabhadra** ​(*samantabhadra*) — ‌Universal Good, ‌Practice ​· 'Universal ​Beneficence' — ​the Bodhisattva ​of ​practice, rider ‌of the ​white ​elephant — ‌belongs to ​the ‌Buddhist tradition, ​where it ‌is ​catalogued under ​the domain ​"Universal Good, ​Practice". ​The name ‌means "'Universal ​Beneficence' ‌— the ​Bodhisattva of ‌practice, ​rider of ‌the white ​elephant"[^1].

‌**Samantabhadra** is ​the bodhisattva ​of practice: ‌if ‌Mañjuśrī wields ‌the sword ​of ​wisdom, Samantabhadra ‌is the ​**goodness ​that actually ‌walks** — ​his ​ten great ‌vows (homage, ​offering, confession, ‌rejoicing, ​dedication...) are ​the Mahāyāna's ​complete ​curriculum of ‌the heart, ‌recited ​daily from ‌Wutai to ​Lhasa.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Samantabhadra** ‌and serves ​its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/samantabhadra/). ​The displayed ​form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ​computed from ‌the displayed ​form itself. ​The ​plain ASCII ‌form *samantabhadra* ​contains ‌the same ​letters: no ‌recovered ​diacritics or ‌special encoding ‌is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Devanagari as ​**समन्तभद्र**. ​Etymologically it ​means "'Universal ​Beneficence' — ​the ‌Bodhisattva of ​practice, rider ​of ‌the white ​elephant"[^1].

The ‌canonical spelling ​**Samantabhadra** ‌matches the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*samantabhadra* contains ‌the same ​letters, ‌so no ​lost diacritics ‌or encoding ​transition ‌is claimed. ​The editorial ‌work is ​to ​fix one ‌reviewed reference ‌spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ​and provenance, ​and keep ‌the ​original evidence ​visible. meditation.body: Samantabhadra ​is the ‌answer to ‌the suspicion ​that ​the Mahāyāna ​is all ​vision and ​no work. ‌The ​Avataṃsaka gives ​us a ‌cosmos of ​jeweled ‌interpenetration — ​and then, ‌in its ​final pages, ​hands ​the whole ​thing to ​a bodhisattva ‌on ​an elephant ‌and ten ​vows. The ‌placement ​is the ‌teaching: contemplation ​without practice ‌is a ​postcard; ​practice is ‌the journey ‌the postcard ‌describes. ​His vows ​are famously ‌unglamorous — ​homage, praise, ​offering, ‌confession, rejoicing ​— none ​of them ‌beyond ​a beginner, ‌all of ​them infinite. ​That ​combination is ​the point: ‌a practice ‌anyone can ​start ‌and no ​one can ​finish is ‌precisely ‌the shape ‌of a ‌life. He ​is also ‌the ​bodhisattva of ​the collective: ​every vow ‌ends ​in dedication, ​the merit ​poured back ‌into ​the common ​account. If ​Mañjuśrī asks ‌what you ​know, ‌Samantabhadra asks ​what you ‌did with ​it ‌— and ‌his elephant ​does not ​hurry, because ​goodness, ​unlike insight, ‌is allowed ‌to take ​forever.[^1]
